title: 2025-07-16-primex-pilot-cost-per-token-review
summary: Weekly POC sync to review pilot economics — tokens/sec/$, observed caching benefits, and tradeoffs between batching and latency. SE presented recent benchmark runs on dedicated vs hosted instances; team agreed to run a 1-hour tail-latency focused benchmark and to exchange updated pricing/throughput sheet.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-16 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: zoom.us/rec/primex-0716 (note: link obfuscated)

Attendees:
- Samira Cho (Redwood, AE)
- Diego Alvarez (Redwood, SE)
- Priya Natarajan (Redwood, CSM)
- Ethan Park (Primex, Head of ML)
- Maya Singh (Primex, Infra)
- Jordan Lee (Primex, Product)
- Rosa Kim (Primex, SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): overall cost down ~18% w/ prefix caching, batching helped throughput but we saw 95th spike on some endpoints when batch size > 8; dedicated pool gives more consistent tokens/sec but costs higher per hour; quantized weights saved ~12% token cost in mix workloads.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, quick roll call — can you hear me?
[00:06] Ethan: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:08] Maya: Good here.
[00:10] Samira: Great. Agenda today — Diego will walk through the latest bench numbers, then we'll talk caching and batching tradeoffs and agree next steps.
[00:18] Diego: Cool. I pushed two runs overnight — one on hosted Redwood API (multi-tenant) and one on dedicated infra (4xA10-like shape, single tenant). Both runs used the same prompt set Maya shared last week but we included a synthetic long-tail of 1k tokens for tail testing.
[00:33] Diego: High level: tokens/sec per dollar improved on hosted when we enabled prefix/K-V cache for repeated prompts — roughly 24% improvement on average for the top 50 prompts. On dedicated, tokens/sec is steadier and peak throughput about 15% higher, but cost per hour is ~2.1x which changes the tokens-per-dollar math.
[00:52] Jordan: Sorry, when you say K-V cache did you mean server side prefix cache or client-side?
[00:56] Diego: Server side, automatic prefix caching in the runtime. I think our logs showed cache hit-rate around 42% for the set you gave us. There were a bunch of near-duplicates which helped.
[01:08] Ethan: 42% is higher than I expected, that's promising. What's the distribution? Is it concentrated in a few prompts?
[01:13] Diego: Yes — top 10 prompts were responsible for ~65% of hits. Long-tail hardly hit at all. That suggests we should focus caching on top routes and maybe warm-cache during peak windows.
[01:25] Rosa: Warm-cache — does that keep memory in the runtime? Any eviction behavior to watch for? We run fairly memory-constrained nodes in staging.
[01:31] Diego: Good question. Cache is an LRU per model variant, and you can set eviction thresholds. For the staging run I left defaults; we'll tune for your memory footprint if you want.
[01:40] Maya: On batching — our product team wants lower per-token cost but product demands sub-200ms P95 for chat quick-replies. We saw P95 go up past 350ms when batch size hit 12.
[01:51] Diego: Right — that's the usual tradeoff. Throughput (tokens/sec) increases sublinearly with batch size; however latency tail suffers when there's load skew and small messages stuck behind big ones.
[02:03] Samira: Can you quantify tokens per dollar across the configurations? A simple number we can use for internal decisioning.
[02:09] Diego: Sure. Using the shared sheet, rough numbers: Hosted w/ caching: 1,600 tokens per $1.00; Hosted no-cache: 1,300 tokens/$1; Dedicated w/ caching: 2,400 tokens/$1 but divided by higher hourly bill — effectively if you normalize to your committed monthly cost it becomes close to 1,900 tokens/$1 if you have sustained load. These are approximate for mixed-length workload (avg seq 240).
[02:31] Ethan: Wait, dedicated shows higher raw tokens/$ but you then normalize based on committed hours. Can you explain the math quickly?
[02:36] Diego: Yeah — raw tokens per dollar on the machine is better because GPU efficiency is higher; but when you add the hourly and reserved price we amortize cost across idle cycles. If utilization is low — say <40% — the effective tokens/$ drops.
[02:49] Jordan: So for bursty usage we might prefer hosted to avoid paying for idle dedicated capacity?
[02:53] Priya: Exactly; also note Redwood has autoscaling and burst capacity options but they change pricing tiers. We'll include those in the pricing sheet.
[03:02] Ethan: Quantization — you mentioned a 12% saving earlier. Which quant level was that? 8-bit? 4-bit?
[03:08] Diego: These runs used 8-bit dynamic quant on the weights and some kernels tuned for that. Quality delta small on your eval set — roughly 0.5% drop on rouge-like metric. We can try 4-bit but need to validate hallucination risk.
[03:20] Maya: Any impact on latency with quantization?
[03:23] Diego: For many models 8-bit reduces compute time slightly, which helps tokens/sec; but for some kernels it adds dequant/requant overhead — so depends on batch size and seq length. Our sheet flags per-model impact.
[03:34] [03:36] — brief crosstalk while someone pulls up the sheet —
[03:45] Ethan: Looking at the sheet now — I see a column "tokens_per_$" and another "95th_latency_ms". For route A we get 1,800 tokens/$ with P95 280ms. For route B (longer) it's 900 tokens/$ and P95 1.1s.
[03:58] Diego: Yup. That suggests focusing caching on route B is lower ROI unless you can shrink seq length or precompute some parts.
[04:07] Jordan: Could we carve out route A for dedicated and keep route B on hosted?
[04:11] Samira: That hybrid routing is exactly what Redwood's smart routing can do — route by latency sensitivity and cost target. We can set policies: route A to dedicated, route B to hosted, and failover to smaller models for B if costs spike.
[04:24] Rosa: One concern: our security team will want private networking for dedicated. How much extra work was that in past pilots?
[04:30] Diego: For a Private or VPC deployment we provision a customer-dedicated control plane or private links — typical onboarding 2–4 weeks depending on compliance checks. We can share a checklist.
[04:40] Maya: On the benchmarking methodology — you mentioned a synthetic long-tail of 1k tokens. Could the long-tail be skewing the dedicated numbers?
[04:46] Diego: It affects peak memory and KV cache utility; dedicated handled it well in throughput but increased tail latency for other short requests when packing happened. That's why I recommended the 1-hour tail-latency focused run to better characterize worst-case.
[04:58] Ethan: Let's schedule that. Diego, can you run the run with two scenarios: batch max 8 and batch max 16, sequentially, and capture 99th and 95th?
[05:05] Diego: Yep — I'll do 3 runs: batch cap 4, 8, 16 to show curve.
[05:09] Maya: Also can you capture per-route cache hit rates and memory usage?
[05:12] Diego: Yes. I'll include hit-rate time series and eviction counts.
[05:15] Jordan: Pricing ask — what's the easiest way for us to compare hosted variable spend vs committed dedicated?
[05:19] Samira: I'll send a revised pricing sheet with a simple calculator row for Effective Tokens/$ assuming different utilization percentages (20/40/60/80%). That should make the tradeoffs explicit.
[05:29] Ethan: On SLOs — our product team wants a guardrail: if P95 for a route exceeds 500ms, fall back to smaller model or cached response. Is that feasible?
[05:37] Diego: Yes, Redwood supports canary and fallback policies. You can configure per-route fallback model or cached response. We'll show config examples.
[05:44] Priya: I'll also add monitoring alert templates to the shared notes for your SREs.
[05:49] Rosa: One more infra question — do you persist KV cache across restarts? We sometimes do rolling restarts and warm-up times matter.
[05:55] Diego: Not persisted by default — it's in-memory cache. There are options to export/restore or a multi-layer cache architecture. For fast warm-up we recommend pre-warming scripts.
[06:05] Ethan: Can you give a quick ROI example — assume our 3 endpoints with combined 50M tokens/day, what savings look like?
[06:13] Diego: Quick back-of-envelope — if caching saves 20% tokens and quantization saves 12% on remaining, combined you'd approximate (1 - 0.2) * (1 - 0.12) ≈ 70% of baseline tokens cost — so ~30% savings. If baseline is $X/day you'll see 30% less. But exact numbers depend on distribution and model choice.
[06:30] Jordan: That framing helps. We need concrete numbers for execs.
[06:33] Samira: I'll include pre-filled scenarios for 30/50/100M tokens/day in the pricing sheet.
[06:38] Ethan: Any gotchas we should be aware of around quality regressions when enabling caching?
[06:42] Diego: If you cache prefixes and the prompt context includes ephemeral session data, caching can surface stale tokens — so avoid caching prompts that embed dynamic session state. We'll help craft rules for cache keys (e.g., hash only of user prompt body, exclude session tokens).
[06:56] Maya: Also, we had compliance ask about logs and PII. How are logs retained and can we purge?
[07:01] Samira: Redwood has configurable retention and can integrate with your KMS; we can enable shorter retention for pilot data and provide audit logs. We'll share the SOC2/ISO docs and a retention config example.
[07:10] Diego: Quick note on measurement noise — when we ran the hosted tests overnight we saw jitter at zone boundaries; suggest running long-duration runs during target traffic windows.
[07:19] Ethan: Okay good.
[07:21] Samira: To recap — Diego will run 3 tail-latency runs (batch 4/8/16) and capture 95/99/evictions and memory; Ethan will share final top-20 prompt variations and confirm P95 targets; Samira will send updated pricing and a scenarios sheet; Priya will add alert templates and tracking.
[07:41] Jordan: Timeline OK — can we reconvene same time next week?
[07:44] Samira: Yes — we can do next Wed same time.
[07:47] Ethan: Works. Thanks everyone.
[07:49] End meeting.
